66159.etyen:
Borrowed from Dutch waker (“wind indicator; buoy”) or Low German waker (“wind indicator; buoy”). The source noun is derived from the nautical verb waken (“to float; remain above water”), which is etymologically the same word as waken (“to be awake; keep watch”). The verb continues Middle Dutch wāken, from Old Dutch wacon, from Proto-Germanic *wakāną (“to be awake, watch”), ultimately from *weǵ- (“to be lively, awake; be strong”).
The Norwegian verb vake (“to float; remain afloat; rise to the surface”) was likewise borrowed from Dutch or Low German and belongs to the same word family as inherit

Compare Danish Ernst, Swedish Ernst, Icelandic Ernst and Faroese Ernst (“male given names”).

1002095.etyen:
First attested in 1750.
Borrowed from German also (“so, therefore; that is”), from Middle High German alsō (“so, thus”), from Old High German alsō (“completely so; exactly so”), from Proto-West Germanic *allswā (“completely so; exactly so, likewise”). The Proto-West Germanic form is composed of *all (“all, entirely”) and *swā (“so, thus”). The Norwegian form was influenced by alt (“all; entirely”).
Compare Danish altså (“so, therefore”), Norwegian Nynorsk altså and altso, Swedish alltså, Dutch alzo (“thus, so”) and English also.

1004655.etyen:

I forbindelse med hundreårsjubileet for spelemannen og folkemusikksamleren Arne Bjørndals fødsel, ble det i 1982 arrangert et fagseminar og en konsert i Bergen.
In connection with the centenary of the birth of fiddler and folk-music collector Arne Bjørndal, a specialist seminar and a concert were held in Bergen in 1982.

1004911.etyen:
From fag (“field, subject”) + seminar (“seminar”), literally “field seminar”.
The first element, fag (“field, subject, discipline”), is borrowed from Middle Low German or Low German fak (“compartment, field”); compare German Fach (“subject, field”). The second element, seminar, is borrowed via German Seminar from Latin sēminārium (“plant nursery; seminary”), from sēmen (“seed”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“to sow”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk fagseminar, Danish fagseminar, Swedish fackseminarium and German Fachseminar (“specialist seminar”).
